pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written mnw; conventionally vocalised “Min”. The name relates to mn, “to be firm, enduring”.
Two consonants, one certain vowel: the oldest god of the eastern desert.

pronunciation.note: Herodotus (2.46) says the Egyptians “are the only people who have a Pan” — Min. The name crossed into Greek without respelling.

domains.title: God of Fertility, the Eastern Desert, and Male Potency
domains.subtitle: The Firm One, Lord of the Processions
domains.lead: Mnw — Min — is the lightning-rod god of male fertility: erect, flail raised, lettuce-crowned, lord of the desert roads to the Red Sea and of everything that stands firm. The Greeks saw Pan in him; the Egyptians saw the power that makes the land and its people endure — mn, the root of his name, means ‘to remain’.

cards.name: The Firm One
cards.desc: His name is the verb “to be enduring”; he is the god of what stands fast — harvests, dynasties, erections.

cards.name: Lord of the Desert Roads
cards.desc: Master of the eastern highlands and the routes to the Red Sea gold mines.

cards.name: Fertility in the Fields
cards.desc: The lettuce — an aphrodisiac to the Egyptians — and the flail of the harvest belong to his iconography.

cards.name: The Processional God
cards.desc: His festival raised his image on its litter in public procession — Egypt’s most ancient god-ritual.

mythology.lead: Min has no narrative myth-cycle; his ‘stories’ are the rituals that stage him — the processions, the erect phallus, the lettuce beds of his gardens — and the oldest continuous cult record of any Egyptian god. His mythology is written in the calendar: his great festival closed the harvest and opened the desert’s travelling season.

myths.title: Older Than the Kings
myths.text: Min’s emblem appears on the artefacts of the late Predynastic — the famous Min-standard carved on the maceheads of King Scorpion and Narmer’s age. Before Horus belonged to the king, Min belonged to the land: the lightning-rod, the ithyphallic pillar, the force that stood behind fertility itself.

myths.title: The Procession at the Harvest
myths.text: His great festival in the month of Shemu opened with the king cutting a sheaf of emmer — the ‘coming forth of Min’ from his shrine on the shoulders of his priests, carried to the acclaim of the crowd, followed by the ritual release of four wild birds to the four winds. The rite married the harvest to virility: the cut grain and the standing god are one mystery.

myths.title: The Only People with a Pan
myths.text: Herodotus describes Min’s procession at Chemmis — the carrying shrine, the phallic imagery — and concludes that the Egyptian Min is the original of the Greek Pan, the same god under two names. It is the earliest comparative-religion argument in Western literature, and it was made about Min.

myths.title: Husband of Repyt and Isis
myths.text: At Coptos he was paired with the lioness-goddess Repyt, ‘the Weary One’ who nonetheless endures; in the wider Osirian orbit his fertility stands behind Horus’ conception. In the Late Period his statue was carried to the graveyards to visit Osiris — the fertility god paying his respects to the dead one, generation greeting dissolution.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks named him Pan without hesitation, and Roman Egypt painted him in both divine dialects at once. Within Egypt he fused with Horus as ‘Min-Horus the victorious’, with Amun-Ra in the Theban Ramesside theology, and with Osiris in the funerary visitations — a god whose essence, enduring potency, annexed whatever it touched.
lore.culturalLegacy: Min’s harvest festival is the ancestor of every ‘first sheaf’ ceremony documented in the Mediterranean; Herodotus’ Pan-equation is still cited as the founding gesture of comparative mythology. Coptos, his city, guarded the desert routes whose exploitation made Egypt’s Eastern Desert gold famous.
lore.extendedMeditation: Mnw: two consonants standing very firmly together. Of all the names in this batch his needs restoration least — Min crossed into Greek and Latin almost unchanged — and that stability is his message: the firm god keeps his form while empires trade his identity between Pan and Min and back again.

sources.name: Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation)
Festival reliefs of the Ramesseum and Medinet Habu (the Min procession)

lore.archaeology: Coptos (Qift) at the Nile’s bend was his city, controlling the desert road to the Red Sea; its temples yielded great Min colossi now in the Ashmolean and Cairo. The Ramesseum’s harvest procession reliefs and Medinet Habu’s festival calendar give his ritual in carved detail, from the cut sheaf to the released birds.
lore.cult: His cult-procession was among Egypt’s oldest public festivals; the pharaoh himself cut the first sheaf before Min’s shrine. In the Late Period, priests carried his statue in a ceremonial circuit of the necropolis — the fertility god blessing the dead with the promise of renewal.
lore.iconography: The ithyphallic mummy-form god, arms raised with flail erect, wearing two tall plumes rising from a red ribbon whose streamers fall behind, standing on a dais hung with lettuce bunches. The Greeks added the syrinx of Pan; the Egyptians never needed it — the plumes were enough.
lore.reception: Pan-Min became a fixture of Greco-Roman Egyptomania, and the frank virility of his images both fascinated and embarrassed early travellers — several of his colossi were re-erected in European museums with discreet repositioning. He is now the standard case-study of how fertility cults met the documentation biases of classical reporters.
